edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page. The template is missing the id.

edits.quote: Find every way to cover each shape with blue blocks. Draw each way in its own copy. [three copies of the small hexagon, which has 2 coverings; four copies of the long hexagon, which has 3]
edits.fix: Name the two shapes ('the small hexagon and the long hexagon'). Then either print exactly 2 and 3 copies, or let the adult know that one copy of each will stay blank. As printed, a K-1 child takes 'done' to mean every copy is filled, so they will draw repeats or rotations of a covering they already have.

edits.quote: Change it into the right picture with as few moves as you can. [example labeled only 'one move']
edits.fix: Say what a move is, as the 4-5 page does: 'A move: lift three blue blocks that make a hexagon and put them back turned the other way, as in the top picture.' Without this, a child or the parent volunteer may count moving any single block as a move. The puzzles themselves check out: they need 2 and 4 moves.

k-1.summary: A solid K-1 set with real content: six actual-size boards to cover or rule out (each impossible board has an even number of triangles), fewest greens on triangles of sides 2 to 5, all coverings of two hexagons, flip puzzles that need 2 and 4 moves, and a block-placing game whose answers are correct (second player wins on the hexagon, first player on the two strips). The diagrams are correct and the text is lean. The page needs a definition of a move in words and recording copies that match the number of answers.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

edits.quote: Which of these boards can be covered with blue blocks only?
edits.fix: Delete the opening question. The two instructions that follow it (cover and draw lines; X the impossible ones) already ask for exactly this.

edits.quote: Each board below is a big hexagon with two gray holes, and no block may cover a hole.
edits.fix: The diagrams already show a big hexagon with two holes. Shorten to 'No block may cover a gray hole.'

edits.quote: Could triangle C in Problem 2 be covered with blue blocks and fewer green triangles than you used? Explain.
edits.fix: The answer depends on what each child happened to use. A child who used 6 answers 'yes' and never meets the bound. Ask for the true minimum and a proof: 'What is the fewest green triangles that triangle C needs? Explain why no covering can use fewer.' Or make it the first case of Problem 5.

grades-2-3.summary: This band develops kernel 1 well, with every board at actual size: covered or X'd boards (B, D, E are unbalanced; G is balanced but still impossible, a good contrast), fewest greens on triangles of sides 2 to 5, hexagons with holes (A and D can each be covered 4 ways; B and C fail the count), a generalization to sides 10 and 100, purple chevrons (4, 5, 4, 5 greens, never fewer than blue), and a design-a-board task. I checked all of these. The only real fix is Problem 4, whose answer depends on the child's own result; the other edits are small trims.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

edits.quote: Blank small drawings of boards are for recording.
edits.fix: Delete. Each problem already says where to draw.

edits.quote: 4 moves / 5 moves / 6 moves / 7 moves, each heading over a column of 4 small hexagons; 'If you run out of copies, you can draw more on the back.'
edits.fix: A 6-move round trip passes through 6 coverings, but its column has only 4 copies, and the back-of-page sentence covers for that. Print one unlabeled pool of at least 10 to 12 copies, or at least 6 per column, and delete the sentence. The math is correct: 4 and 6 are possible, 5 and 7 are not.

edits.quote: If you run out of copies, you can draw more on the back.
edits.fix: Delete. There are 24 copies and the big hexagon has 20 coverings.

grades-4-5.summary: This band follows kernel 2 from all 6 coverings of a small hexagon, through the flip graph, shortest flip routes (8 and 4 moves; I verified both), round trips (4 and 6 possible, 5 and 7 not), and chains (I checked the drawn coverings, and the four chain pairs split two possible, two impossible), up to proofs of shortest routes and parity and counting 20 coverings of two different boards. It is more than enough for an hour, and every problem does work. The only edits are the short 6-move recording column in Problem 4 and two meta sentences.

overall.strongest: Grades 2-3 builds the coloring obstruction step by step on correct, actual-size boards: possible and impossible boards (including a balanced but impossible one), boards with holes, fewest greens generalized to sides 10 and 100, chevrons, and a design-a-board task.
overall.weakest: No band has a serious flaw. The weakest points are small: K-1 Problem 5 never says in words what a move is, grades 2-3 Problem 4's answer depends on the child's own result, and the 6-move column in grades 4-5 Problem 4 has too few copies.
